title: Redis: one fast server, many data structures
dek: Most people meet Redis as a cache, but it is a server of data structures kept in memory: strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams. Here is what each is for, why one command never interrupts another, how it keeps data across a restart, and how a cluster splits keys over machines.

body.cap: Every command changes one structure on the server, in one step. That is why a cart, a ranking or a rate limit needs no locks in your code.

items: Strings hold any value up to 512 MB, usually a serialised object, with an optional expiry (`EX 300`).
Hashes hold fields inside one key, so a cart can change one dish without rewriting the whole cart.
Sorted sets keep members ordered by a score; `ZREVRANGE top:pune 0 9` returns the top 10 at once, which is why leaderboards use them.
Streams are append-only logs with consumer groups, like a small Kafka inside Redis. Plain pub/sub, by contrast, delivers only to whoever is listening at that moment and keeps nothing.

Geo commands keep points in a sorted set, scored by geohash, and find members within a radius: one quick way to answer "restaurants near me". The concept 'Finding what's nearby' compares the other ways.

body.label: ZOTATO · THREE JOBS IN REDIS
body.x:
# today's top restaurants in Pune
ZINCRBY top:pune:2026-11-08 1 r42
ZREVRANGE top:pune:2026-11-08 0 9 WITHSCORES

# at most 5 OTPs per phone per hour
INCR otp:9800000001                 # returns the count so far
EXPIRE otp:9800000001 3600 NX       # start the hour on the first request only

# restaurants within 3 km, nearest first
GEOADD rest:pune 73.8567 18.5204 r42
GEOSEARCH rest:pune FROMLONLAT 73.85 18.52 BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 20

Redis runs commands on a single thread (newer versions use extra threads for network reads and writes, not for commands). Two clients incrementing the same counter can't interleave, so `INCR` is safe without a lock. Several commands can run as one unit with `MULTI`/`EXEC`, or as a Lua script, which also runs without interruption.

items: The flip side: one slow command stalls everyone. `KEYS *` on lakhs of keys, deleting a huge set, or a long Lua script blocks the server for every other client. Use `SCAN` to walk keys and `UNLINK` to delete big ones in the background.
One CPU core per node is the ceiling for commands, so scale out with more nodes, not a bigger machine.

body.x: Replication to a replica is asynchronous, so a failover can also lose the last writes the replica hadn't received. Sentinel watches a primary and its replicas and promotes one when the primary dies; managed services do the same for you.

body.cap: The client does the routing: it knows which node owns each slot, so a request takes one hop, and MOVED corrects it after slots change hands.

items: Commands that touch several keys work only when all the keys are in the same slot. Put the shared part in braces, a hash tag: `{user:77}:cart` and `{user:77}:profile` land in the same slot.
A hash tag that everyone shares puts all of it on one node, so use it for small groups of keys, not for a whole feature.
Replicas can serve reads, but they lag a little behind, as replicas always do.

body.x: Where it fits, and where it doesn't

items: Good: caching, sessions, rate limits, leaderboards, counters, short-lived locks with an expiry, deduplicating recent events, small queues.
Careful: anything that must survive a crash with no loss, data bigger than memory, and queries you can't express as a key lookup.
Memory is the bill. Set `maxmemory` and an eviction policy (`allkeys-lru` for a cache) so a full server evicts instead of refusing writes.

In 2024 Redis moved to a more restrictive licence and the Linux Foundation started Valkey, a compatible open-source fork; in 2025 Redis added an open-source (AGPL) option again. Managed clouds offer one or both; the commands are the same.

items: Name the structure, not just 'Redis': a sorted set for the leaderboard, a hash for the cart, `INCR` plus `EXPIRE` for the rate limit.
Say what happens if Redis restarts: a cache refills from the database; anything else needs a source of truth elsewhere.
Mention hot keys and big keys, and that one slow command blocks all others.
For more than one node, say Redis Cluster with 16,384 slots, or client-side sharding.
Where it appears here: the Leaderboard problem ranks players with sorted sets, and Restaurants near me keeps live open/closed status in Redis.

body.label: Go deeper: a lock in Redis, and its limits

body.x: `SET lock:payout:42 owner-17 NX PX 30000` takes a lock only if nobody holds it, with a 30-second expiry. Release it only if you still own it, with a short Lua script that checks the value before deleting. This is fine to stop two workers doing the same harmless job at once.

It is not safe for correctness on its own: a worker can pause past the expiry while another takes the lock. When a duplicate would do damage, add a fencing token checked by the system you write to, as the Contention concept explains.
